Like DcUtf, but begins with magic DcMM\0 followed by UUID d5ab819e-9b8e-4d61-adbc-933e8851e79a as 16 binary bytes. Every top-level Dc 203 is followed by a type byte and a 128-bit big-endian payload-byte length, including zero-length payloads. Type 2 then carries a 128-bit big-endian metadata-byte length, followed by that many DcUtf bytes encoding [type]? [checksum]?, then the raw binary payload. The checksum covers the raw payload bytes; its hash type is declared in the checksum's own Dc 203 frame. The metadata block may be empty. The terminating Dc 204 is implicit. Writers of binary and typed-checksum encapsulations use type 2; textual Dc 203 writers emit base64 payload Dcs with the decoded payload-byte length and preserve declared types and checksums. DcUtf payload bytes can use type 2 with a declared DcUtf type; they are not spliced into the surrounding character stream. Legacy type 0 stores raw binary and type 3 adds a 32-byte binary SHA-256 checksum following the payload length; both remain readable. Types 1 and 4 are retired: their original intent was, I believe, to indicate the encoding of the stored data (which it is to be interpreted as), but the original implementation used them to indicate the encoding in which the data was stored (and emitted non-encapsulation Dcs inside Dc 203, which would be invalid syntax). The use cases for them can be met by using type byte 2 with type metadata. As type bytes 1 and 4 were never used, readers reject either byte with an explicit unsupported-legacy-type error rather than interpreting or converting its ambiguous payload. Writers must not emit types 1 or 4. Type bytes 5..255 are reserved.
